Title: A Review on Shaping Chatbot Personalities via Large Language Models
Authors: Chang, T. and Hung, S. and Chen, Y. and Chang, N. and Ku, C. H. and Lin, S. Y. and Chien, S. Y. J.
Statistical Methods Used: N/A
Summary of Results: ‘Prompt engineering offers flexibility and simplicity but also presents challenges. For example, the lack of explicit prompt examples can lead to inconsistent model outputs, especially in complex scenarios.  Fine-tuning is an effective method for aligning LLM outputs with specific personality profiles. By adjusting parameters and training on personalityannotated datasets, fine-tuning can significantly enhance the personalization of user interactions. However, the risk of overfitting poses a significant drawback. Overfitting can make the model too rigidly aligned with a specific personality, reinforcing biases or stereotypes and potentially alienating users who do not resonate with this fixed personality. Unsupervised machine learning methods provide flexibility in shaping LLM personalities without direct human annotation. However, this flexibility often comes at the cost of precision. These methods may capture unintended correlations or noise within the data, leading to imprecise representations of personality traits. Knowledge editing allows targeted adjustments to a model’s knowledge base to align with desired personality traits while maintaining overall model performance. However, this method faces limitations, such as the difficulty in accurately editing certain personality traits and the uncertainty of manipulation effects when using models with a large number of parameters (e.g., over 10B parameters). Ethical concerns also arise, particularly regarding the potential occurrence of offensive language or discriminatory content, which may not be fully avoided through this method.’

Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons.
Logistic regression for significance testing.

Summary of Results: Results showed that (1) explicit but not implicit personas replicated human perceptions in the annotation task, (2) explicit personas were sometimes able to generate text which reflected subjective human opinions, and (3) implicit personas showed a general lack of agreement with explicit personas and, more importantly, known human perceptions. Prompt Architecture/Methodology:
Explicit prompts: "You are a 78-year-old female," "You are politically conservative."
Implicit prompts: Names tied to demographics ("Your name is Ethel") or cultural cues (e.g., "You play video games").
Research Questions:
RQ1: Do personified LLMs replicate known human perception and belief patterns?
RQ2: How do explicit/implicit personas influence LLM output across domains (e.g., age, gender, political ideology)?
RQ3: Which human factors are most critical in shaping LLM responses?

Type: Novel method or framework for persona implementation
Keywords**: Steering vectors, LLM prompting, personas, domain alignment
Title: Can Role Vectors Affect LLM Behaviour?
Authors: Daniele Potertì, Andrea Seveso, Fabio Mercorio
LLMs Used: LLaMa3-Instruct, Llama-3.1.8B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen-7B-Chat, Qwen-1.8B, Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B
Statistical Methods Used:
Difference-in-means for role vector extraction from the residual stream
- Benchmark accuracy comparisons on MMLU (2,457 questions across 8 domains)
- 70/30 validation–test split
- Activation addition and directional ablation as experimental interventions
- Statistical significance with p-values (p ≤ 0.05, ≤ 0.01, ≤ 0.001)
- Patch scoping procedure to assess whether the model "identifies" as a role, Spearman correlation
Summary of Results:
Role vector activation outperforms persona-based prompting, as noted in prior work by Zheng et al. (2024). Role vectors demonstrably influence LLM behavior. Activation addition improves
in-domain task performance—especially in larger models and deeper layers—and
sometimes produces unexpected cross-domain gains. Directional ablation causes
measurable performance drops, confirming these vectors are causally active.
Internal activation manipulation outperforms traditional persona-based
prompting, which has no effect or a slightly negative impact on objective
tasks.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology:
128 synthetic prompts generated per role. Not traditional prompting. A difference-in-means vector is computed by
contrasting model activations on 128 role-specific prompts (generated by
Claude 3.5 Haiku) vs. 128 generic Alpaca baseline prompts. The resulting role
vector is inserted directly into the model's residual stream via either
activation addition (α·d added to activations at a chosen layer) or
directional ablation (the role direction is projected out entirely). No system
prompt or persona instruction is used during inference.
Research Questions:
RQ1: Can we identify specific latent role directions, encoded as role
vectors, within the activation space that, when leveraged, lead to improved
performance on objective tasks?
- RQ2: Do the directions that enhance performance effectively impersonate the
role of interest?
- RQ3: If we eliminate these directions in the models, do their performances
suffer as a consequence?

Type: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation
Keywords**: LLM-as-a-judge, MT-bench, Chatbot Arena, human preference, pairwise comparison, position bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement bias, chatbot evaluation
Title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
Authors: Zheng, Lianmin; Chiang, Wei-Lin; Sheng, Ying; Zhuang, Siyuan; Wu, Zhanghao; Zhuang, Yonghao; Lin, Zi; Li, Zhuohan; Li, Dacheng; Xing, Eric; Zhang, Hao; Gonzalez, Joseph E.; Stoica, Ion
LLMs Used: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude-v1, Vicuna-13B, Alpaca-13B, LLaMA-13B
Human Participants?: Y - 58 expert human labelers rated MT-bench questions; 2114 unique crowdsourced voters on Chatbot Arena
Statistical Methods Used: Agreement rate (probability of random same-type judges agreeing), average win rate, position bias consistency percentage, failure rate under verbosity attack
Summary of Results: Strong LLMs such as GPT-4 can serve as scalable judges of open-ended chatbot responses, achieving over 80% agreement with human expert preferences on MT-bench and matching crowdsourced human agreement on Chatbot Arena. The study identifies three main bias types in LLM judges—position bias, verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias—and shows that position bias can be mitigated by swapping answer order and using reference-guided grading. GPT-4 single-answer grading is found to be a scalable and explainable alternative to pairwise comparison, correlating well with human preferences across model categories.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Three judge formats tested: (1) pairwise comparison — judge presented with a question and two answers, asked to pick the better one; (2) single answer grading — judge assigns a score on a scale of 1–10 to a single response; (3) reference-guided grading — judge first generates its own answer as a reference before grading. Multi-turn questions presented as full two-turn conversations in a single prompt. Chain-of-thought and few-shot variants also explored.
Research Questions: Can strong LLMs serve as scalable and accurate judges to evaluate other LLMs on open-ended questions? What are the key biases and limitations of LLM-as-a-judge, and how can they be mitigated? How well do LLM judges agree with human preferences on MT-bench and Chatbot Arena?

Type: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation
Keywords**: LLM-as-a-Judge, human-centered design, EvaluLLM, evaluation criteria, NLG evaluation, human-in-the-loop, pairwise comparison, trust, customizable metrics
Title: Human-Centered Design Recommendations for LLM-as-a-Judge
Authors: Pan, Q. and Ashktorab, Z. and Desmond, M. and Cooper, M. S. and Johnson, J. and Nair, R. and Geyer, W.
Human Participants?: Y - 8 industry professional domain experts (data scientists, software engineers, AI engineers) participated in semi-structured think-aloud interviews using the EvaluLLM prototype
Statistical Methods Used: Qualitative thematic analysis (independent coding by two authors, codebook development, theme merging); agreement rate between human and LLM-as-a-judge reported as a UI feature
Summary of Results: A user study of the EvaluLLM tool revealed that practitioners face significant challenges in defining effective evaluation criteria for LLM-as-a-judge systems, including difficulty articulating criteria upfront and needing multiple iterative refinements. Participants valued customizable, structured evaluation templates and desired per-criterion performance breakdowns rather than a single aggregate win rate. The study produced human-centered design recommendations emphasizing efficient criteria iteration, structured templates, interactive refinement, and transparency mechanisms to build trust in LLM-based evaluations.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: EvaluLLM uses a pairwise comparison approach: users define custom evaluation criteria in natural language, a selected LLM judge compares pairs of model outputs against those criteria, and results are surfaced with rationales. A blind review process hides model identities during human spot-checks. No fixed system prompt format specified; freeform natural language criteria input is the design focus.
Research Questions: What challenges do practitioners encounter when using LLM-as-a-judge tools for model evaluation? What design recommendations can support human-AI collaboration in LLM evaluation workflows to ensure criteria alignment with human intent and trustworthy results?

Type: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation
Keywords**: LLM-as-a-Judge, alignment tasks, position bias, length bias, flipping noise, self-inconsistency, explainable metrics, prompt templates, pairwise evaluation, TL;DR summarization, HH-RLHF
Title: Systematic Evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge in LLM Alignment Tasks: Explainable Metrics and Diverse Prompt Templates
Authors: Wei, H.; He, S.; Xia, T.; Liu, F.; Wong, A.; Lin, J.; Han, M.
Statistical Methods Used: Accuracy (Acc_both, Acc_random), position bias score (PB), length bias score (LB), self-consistent rate (SCR), flipping probability (q), stratified sampling; mean and standard deviation across five splits
Summary of Results: Prompt template choice has a significant impact on LLM judge performance, with the same model exhibiting markedly different accuracy, position bias, and length bias depending on which of up to ten templates is used. All tested LLM judges show only mediocre alignment with human evaluators on both the TL;DR summarization and HH-RLHF-Helpfulness datasets (all accuracies below 0.7), underscoring that human evaluation is still necessary for precise comparison of alignment systems. The paper introduces theoretically interpretable metrics—accuracy, position bias, and length bias with explicit denoising for self-inconsistency—and an open-source evaluation framework to help practitioners select appropriate LLM judges.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Pairwise comparison format: judge is presented with a prompt and two candidate responses (in both orders) and selects the preferred response. Eight prompt templates (for summarization) and ten templates (for helpfulness) sourced from published alignment papers are tested. Temperature set to 0.1; each sample evaluated five times per position to estimate flipping probability.
Research Questions: How do different prompt templates affect LLM judge reliability (accuracy, position bias, length bias) on alignment tasks? What is the true alignment level between LLM judges and human evaluators on common alignment datasets? How can self-inconsistency (flipping noise) be formally modeled and mitigated in LLM judge evaluation metrics?

Type: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation
Keywords**: LLM-as-a-Judge, bias correction, sensitivity, specificity, confidence interval, calibration, statistical reporting, win rate, Chatbot Arena
Title: How to Correctly Report LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations
Authors: Lee, C.; Zeng, T.; Jeong, J.; Sohn, J.Y.; Lee, K.
LLMs Used: GPT-4.1-mini, Claude-Opus-4.6, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Claude-Haiku-4.5, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-nano, Gemini-3-Flash
Human Participants?: Y - human-preference labels from Chatbot Arena used as ground truth for calibration and validation
Statistical Methods Used: Bias-corrected point estimator (misclassification-adjusted estimator), 95% confidence intervals (adjusted Wald method), delta method for variance, adaptive allocation strategy, Monte Carlo simulation (10,000 replications), sensitivity (q1) and specificity (q0) estimation
Summary of Results: The naive practice of reporting the raw fraction of LLM-judged correct responses as the true accuracy is systematically biased due to imperfect LLM judge sensitivity and specificity, and existing bias-correction methods fail under distribution shift between test and calibration datasets. The authors propose a misclassification-adjusted estimator with confidence intervals that remains unbiased under such distributional shifts, and an adaptive calibration allocation strategy that reduces interval length. Empirical validation on Chatbot Arena shows the proposed estimator reduces bias across six target models compared to the naive estimator, and the framework can achieve lower variance than human-only evaluation when judge accuracy is sufficiently high.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Not a prompt design paper; the framework is a statistical plug-in correction layer applied on top of any existing LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. The judge (e.g., GPT-4.1-mini) is used in standard pairwise or binary evaluation mode; a small human-labeled calibration set is used to estimate judge sensitivity and specificity for bias correction.
Research Questions: Why is the standard practice of reporting raw LLM-judged accuracy statistically biased, and how can this bias be corrected? Under what parameter regimes (judge sensitivity/specificity, true accuracy) does bias-corrected LLM-as-a-judge evaluation achieve lower variance than human-only evaluation? How can confidence intervals be constructed that remain valid under distribution shift between test and calibration datasets?

Type: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation
Keywords**: cognitive bias, LLM evaluators, CoBBLEr benchmark, order bias, egocentric bias, compassion fade, salience bias, bandwagon effect, attentional bias, Rank-Biased Overlap, pairwise preference
Title: Benchmarking Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models as Evaluators
Authors: Koo, Ryan; Lee, Minhwa; Raheja, Vipul; Park, Jong Inn; Kim, Zae Myung; Kang, Dongyeop
LLMs Used: GPT-4, ChatGPT, InstructGPT, LLaMAv2-70B, LLaMA-65B, Cohere-54B, Falcon-40B, Alpaca-13B, Vicuna-13B, OpenAssistant-12B, Mistral-7B, OLMO-7B, Baize-7B, Koala-7B, WizardLM-7B, MPT-7B
Human Participants?: Y - 6 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers provided 300 human preference annotations for comparison with model evaluations
Statistical Methods Used: Rank-Biased Overlap (RBO), bias proportion vs. random threshold, chi-square / proportion significance test (Appendix B.5), inter-annotator agreement via RBO
Summary of Results: The CoBBLEr benchmark evaluates 16 LLMs across six cognitive biases (order, compassion fade, egocentric, salience, bandwagon, and attentional) and finds that approximately 40% of comparisons made by all models exhibit at least one bias, with no model reliably serving as an unbiased evaluator. The average Rank-Biased Overlap (RBO) between LLM evaluation rankings and human preference rankings is only 44%, indicating substantial misalignment between machine and human judgment. Larger models are not systematically less biased, and induced biases (bandwagon, attentional) affect even frontier models severely.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Pairwise evaluation format: evaluator model is prompted with an instruction and two anonymized model responses (System Star vs. System Square) and asked which is better based on coherence and alignment with the instruction. Each pair is evaluated twice with positions swapped. For induced biases, additional information (fake majority statistic, irrelevant distractor sentence) is inserted into the prompt. For compassion fade, real model names replace aliases.
Research Questions: Do LLMs exhibit cognitive biases analogous to human cognitive biases when used as automatic evaluators? How well do LLM evaluations align with human preferences? Can a standardized benchmark (CoBBLEr) measure six distinct implicit and induced biases in LLM-as-a-judge settings?

Type: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation
Keywords**: LLM-as-a-Judge, bias quantification, CALM framework, position bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement bias, compassion-fade, bandwagon, authority bias, sentiment bias, diversity bias, fallacy-oversight, chain-of-thought, refinement-aware, robustness rate
Title: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge
Authors: Ye, J. and Wang, Y. and Huang, Y. and Chen, D. and Zhang, Q. and Moniz, N. and Zhang, X.
LLMs Used: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-turbo), GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o, GLM-4, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Qwen2-72B-Instruct
Statistical Methods Used: Robustness Rate (RR), Consistency Rate (CR), original accuracy (Acc_ori), hacked accuracy (Acc_hack), ErrorRate_SE (self-enhancement), ErrorRate_RA (refinement-aware), Z-score normalization for self-enhancement heat map
Summary of Results: The CALM framework systematically quantifies 12 distinct bias types in LLM-as-a-Judge systems using automated principle-guided perturbation, finding that all six tested advanced LLMs exhibit significant vulnerabilities across multiple bias categories. Claude-3.5 shows the greatest overall resilience to biases while ChatGPT is most susceptible to position and bandwagon effects; no single model is uniformly best across all bias types, indicating that bias profiles are model- and task-specific. The study also finds that biases are more pronounced on alignment datasets than fact-related datasets, and that chain-of-thought prompting generally improves judgment accuracy but to varying degrees across models.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Judgment prompts follow the format P = (I, Q, R) for scoring tasks or P = (I, Q, R1, R2) for pairwise comparison, based on templates from Zheng et al. (2024) and Liu et al. (2023a) with slight modifications. Biases are injected via automated perturbation — an LLM (GPT-4o) modifies either the response R or instruction I according to bias-specific guidelines (e.g., lengthening responses for verbosity bias, inserting fake citations for authority bias, adding identity markers to system prompt for diversity bias). Temperature set to 0.7.
Research Questions: What are the 12 distinct types of bias that can undermine the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge systems? Can biases be quantified automatically without human evaluation? How do different advanced LLMs compare in their robustness to these biases across scoring and pairwise comparison tasks?

Type: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation
Keywords**: LLM-as-a-Judge, judge alignment, TriviaQA, exam-taker models, Scott's pi, percent agreement, leniency bias, prompt sensitivity, false positives, false negatives, precision, recall
Title: Judging the Judges: Evaluating Alignment and Vulnerabilities in LLMs-as-Judges
Authors: Thakur, A. S. and Choudhary, K. and Ramayapally, V. S. and Vaidyanathan, S. and Hupkes, D.
LLMs Used: GPT-4 Turbo, Llama-2-7B, Llama-2-13B, Llama-2-70B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-3-70B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, Gemma-2B, Mistral-7B, JudgeLM-7B
Human Participants?: Y - 3 human judges annotated 1,200 randomly sampled TriviaQA responses; inter-human alignment = 96.2% Scott's pi
Statistical Methods Used: Scott's pi coefficient, percent agreement, Spearman rank correlation, precision, recall, leniency bias estimation (P_c and P_+), bootstrapping for sample size validation
Summary of Results: In a controlled TriviaQA evaluation setting with near-perfect human agreement, only the largest judge models (GPT-4 Turbo, Llama-3-70B, Llama-3.1-70B) achieve strong alignment with humans as measured by Scott's pi, yet even these best judges still differ from human scores by up to 5 points and exhibit leniency bias. Percent agreement is found to be a misleading metric because models with high percent agreement can still assign very different scores, while Scott's pi better discriminates judge quality. Smaller models are more prone to false positives, more sensitive to prompt complexity, and more easily fooled by dummy answers such as 'Yes' or 'Sure', highlighting that caution is warranted even when alignment appears high.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Judge models receive a prompt containing the TriviaQA question, a list of acceptable reference answers, and the exam-taker model's response, and are instructed to respond with a single word: 'correct' or 'incorrect'. Four prompt variants of varying length and specificity (45 to 301 tokens) are tested, ranging from minimal instructions to detailed guidelines with examples. Few-shot examples drawn from TriviaQA training set. Judge prompts built from human annotation guidelines (Appendix G).
Research Questions: How well do LLM judge models align with human evaluators in a clean, high-agreement evaluation setting? Does percent agreement adequately capture judge quality, or is a more robust metric (Scott's pi) needed? What are the systematic vulnerabilities of LLM judges, including sensitivity to prompt design, leniency bias, and susceptibility to dummy answers?

Type: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation
Keywords**: position bias, LLM-as-a-Judge, MT-Bench, DevBench, repetition stability, position consistency, preference fairness, evaluation metrics, pairwise evaluation
Title: Judging the Judges: A Systematic Study of Position Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
Authors: Shi, L. and Ma, C. and Liang, W. and Diao, X. and Ma, W. and Vosoughi, S.
LLMs Used: GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude-2, Claude-instant-1, Gemini-Pro, LLaMA-2-70B-chat, LLaMA-2-13B-chat, LLaMA-2-7B-chat, Vicuna-33B, Vicuna-13B, Vicuna-7B, WizardLM-70B, WizardLM-13B, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Qwen-7B-chat
Statistical Methods Used:
- Repetition Stability (RS): proportion of consistent verdicts when same pair is presented twice
- Position Consistency (PC): proportion of consistent verdicts when positions are swapped
- Preference Fairness (PF): balance of first-position vs second-position preferences
- Win rate calculations across judge-model pairs
- Consistency and bias rate aggregations across >150,000 instances
Summary of Results: This systematic study examines position bias across 15 LLM judges evaluated on MT-Bench and DevBench using over 150,000 evaluation instances. The authors introduce three novel metrics—Repetition Stability (RS), Position Consistency (PC), and Preference Fairness (PF)—to quantify different facets of position bias. Results show that most LLMs exhibit significant position bias, with a general tendency to favor responses placed in the first position. GPT-4 demonstrates the least position bias while smaller open-source models show the most. The study reveals that position bias is pervasive across model families and scales, undermining the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge frameworks without explicit debiasing.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Pairwise comparison prompt presents two candidate responses (Response A and Response B) to a given instruction; asks the judge to determine which response is better; position of responses is systematically swapped to measure consistency; both single-round and multi-round conversation evaluation settings tested; prompts follow MT-Bench evaluation protocol.
Research Questions: How prevalent is position bias across different LLM judges at varying scales and families? Can novel metrics (RS, PC, PF) reliably quantify position bias? What factors (model size, family, training method) correlate with reduced position bias?

Type: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation
Keywords**: shortcut bias, LLM-as-a-Judge, provenance cues, recency cues, Verdict Shift Rate, Cue Acknowledgment Rate, unfaithful reasoning, chain-of-thought
Title: The Silent Judge: Unacknowledged Shortcut Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
Authors: Marioriyad, A. and Rohban, M. H. and Soleymani Baghshah, M.
LLMs Used: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, Mistral-Large
Statistical Methods Used:
- Verdict Shift Rate (VSR): proportion of cases where judge changes verdict after cue injection
- Cue Acknowledgment Rate (CAR): proportion of cases where judge explicitly mentions the cue in its reasoning
- McNemar's test for statistical significance of verdict shifts
- Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals
- Analysis split by cue type (provenance: HUMAN/EXPERT/LLM/UNKNOWN; recency: OLD 1950/NEW 2025)
Summary of Results: This paper investigates whether LLM judges rely on illegitimate shortcut cues—specifically provenance cues (labeling a response as written by a HUMAN, EXPERT, LLM, or UNKNOWN source) and recency cues (labeling content as OLD from 1950 or NEW from 2025)—rather than genuine quality assessment. Across 6 LLMs evaluated on 1,200 instances, all models show significant Verdict Shift Rates when cues are injected, yet low Cue Acknowledgment Rates reveal that models rarely explicitly acknowledge the cues in their chain-of-thought. This unfaithful reasoning—where verdicts shift but reasoning does not reflect the cue—demonstrates that LLM judges exploit shortcuts silently, undermining the trustworthiness of their evaluations even when they appear to reason carefully.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Pairwise evaluation prompt augmented with shortcut cues inserted into response metadata or preamble; provenance cues prepended as bracketed labels (e.g., '[Written by a HUMAN expert]'); recency cues embedded as date stamps (e.g., '[Published in 1950]' vs '[Published in 2025]'); chain-of-thought reasoning elicited before final verdict; baseline condition uses identical prompts without any cue injection.
Research Questions: Do LLM judges shift verdicts in response to illegitimate provenance and recency cues? When verdict shifts occur, do judges explicitly acknowledge the influencing cues in their reasoning (faithful vs. unfaithful shortcut use)? Which cue types (provenance vs. recency, specific labels) elicit the strongest bias?

Title: Humans or LLMs as the Judge? A Study on Judgement Biases
Authors: Chen, G. H. and Chen, S. and Liu, Z. and Jiang, F. and Wang, B.
LLMs Used: GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude-2, Claude-instant, Gemini-Pro, LLaMA-2-70B-chat, LLaMA-2-13B-chat, Vicuna-13B, WizardLM-13B, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Qwen-7B-chat
Human Participants?: Y - 60 human judges recruited to evaluate response pairs across the same bias conditions as LLM judges, enabling direct human-LLM comparison on position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference bias, and style bias
Statistical Methods Used:
- Bias rate calculation per judge per bias type
- Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons
- Cohen's kappa for inter-annotator agreement
- Bidirectional stepwise regression with AIC for identifying predictors of bias
- Pairwise vs. list-wise comparison settings compared
- Aggregated bias scores across 4 bias types
Summary of Results: This study compares 4 types of evaluative bias (position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference bias, style bias) across 60 human judges and 11 LLM judges. Results show that both humans and LLMs exhibit all four bias types, but to different degrees: LLMs show stronger self-preference and verbosity biases than humans, while humans show stronger position bias in some conditions. Among LLMs, larger and more capable models (GPT-4, Claude-2) demonstrate lower overall bias. The paper finds that pairwise comparison settings reduce certain biases compared to list-wise settings, and bidirectional stepwise regression identifies model family, size, and instruction-tuning as significant predictors of bias magnitude.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Pairwise comparison prompts administered under controlled bias conditions: (1) position bias — same pair with A/B order swapped; (2) verbosity bias — one response artificially lengthened; (3) self-preference bias — judge evaluates its own vs. another model's output; (4) style bias — responses reformatted with different stylistic markers; human judges received identical prompts via crowdsourcing platform; LLM judges queried via API with temperature=0.
Research Questions: Do LLMs exhibit the same four bias types as human judges? Which bias types are more pronounced in LLMs versus humans? What model characteristics predict lower evaluative bias? Do pairwise vs. list-wise comparison formats affect bias rates?

Keywords**: bias mitigation, LLM-as-a-Judge, debiasing strategies, position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference bias, style bias, calibrated rubric, chain-of-thought, position swap
Title: Judging the Judges: A Systematic Evaluation of Bias Mitigation Strategies in LLM-as-a-Judge Pipelines
Authors: Soumik, S. K.
Statistical Methods Used:
- Bias reduction rate per strategy per bias type
- Win rate delta between biased and debiased conditions
- Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals
- Statistical significance testing across 9 strategies × 5 judges × 3 benchmarks × 4 bias types
- Combined budget analysis for cost-effectiveness
Summary of Results: This paper provides the most comprehensive systematic comparison of bias mitigation strategies for LLM-as-a-Judge to date, testing 9 debiasing approaches (position swap, calibrated rubric, chain-of-thought prompting, and combinations thereof) across 5 LLM judges on 3 benchmarks targeting 4 bias types. Results show that no single strategy eliminates all bias types simultaneously: position swap effectively reduces position bias but can increase verbosity bias; calibrated rubrics reduce style and verbosity bias but are less effective for position bias; chain-of-thought prompting provides modest improvements across all types; combined strategies offer the best overall debiasing but at higher computational cost. The paper introduces a combined budget framework to help practitioners select cost-effective debiasing strategies given resource constraints.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Nine prompt variants tested: (1) baseline pairwise; (2) position swap (A/B then B/A averaged); (3) calibrated rubric with explicit quality dimensions; (4) chain-of-thought with structured reasoning steps; (5) role-specification instructing judge to be unbiased; (6) few-shot examples of unbiased judgments; (7) combined position swap + rubric; (8) combined position swap + CoT; (9) combined rubric + CoT; all variants use temperature=0.
Research Questions: Which debiasing strategies most effectively reduce each of the four bias types? Do combined strategies outperform individual strategies? What are the cost-effectiveness trade-offs across debiasing approaches? Do mitigation effects generalize across judge models and benchmarks?

Title: PersonaEval: Are LLM Evaluators Human Enough to Judge Role-Play?
Authors: Zhou, L. and Zhang, J. and Gao, J. and Jiang, M. and Wang, D.
LLMs Used: GPT-3.5-turbo, Qwen-max, Qwen2.5-32B, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1-distill-Qwen-32B, GPT-o3-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Doubao-1.5-pro, Qwen3-235B, Kimi-K2, QwQ-32B, Grok-3-beta, GPT-4.1, GLM-4.5, Gemini-2.5-flash, Claude-3.7-sonnet, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini-2.5-pro
Human Participants?: Y - 20 volunteers (10 undergrads + 10 PhD students) evaluated 50 examples each from PersonaEval-Literary, Drama, Expertise tracks
Statistical Methods Used:
- Top-1 accuracy (primary metric)
- Top-2 accuracy
- Mean Rank (MR)
- Expected Calibration Error (ECE)
- Brier Score (BS)
- Few-shot prompting (1-shot, 3-shot, 5-shot)
- Self-consistency majority voting (MV-3, MV-5)
Summary of Results: PersonaEval is the first benchmark testing whether LLM evaluators can reliably identify character roles from dialogue context — a necessary prerequisite for credible role-play evaluation. Three tracks (Literary: 26,208 cases from 771 novels; Drama: 1,658 Chinese screenplay snippets; Expertise: 699 Wired '5 Levels' instructional dialogues) present a constrained 4-way classification task with semantically challenging adversarial distractors. State-of-the-art LLMs reach at most 68.8% accuracy (Gemini-2.5-pro), far below the 90.8% achieved by human participants. Fine-tuning on role-specific data degrades performance; few-shot prompting yields modest consistent gains; self-consistency adds negligible benefit. Reasoning models outperform non-reasoning models, pointing to test-time compute as the most promising improvement direction.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Single-turn classification prompt: presents a two-turn dialogue between Character1 (known identity) and Character2 (unknown); provides four candidate role profiles with detailed character descriptions; instructs evaluator to assign Bayesian probability distribution summing to 1 across the four candidates; outputs JSON with candidate names as keys and probabilities as values; candidate order randomized to mitigate position bias.
Research Questions: Can LLM evaluators reliably identify character roles from dialogue context (a prerequisite for human-aligned role-play evaluation)? Do training-time adaptation (fine-tuning on role data) or test-time compute (few-shot, self-consistency) improve role identification? Why do LLMs lag behind humans on this task?

Title: Quantifying and Mitigating Self-Preference Bias of LLM Judges
Authors: Yang, J. and Hu, Z. and Qiu, C. and Deng, Z. and Jiao, X. and Zhou, T.
LLMs Used: Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Grok-4-Fast, Grok-3-Mini, DeepSeek-V3-0324, DeepSeek-V3.2, DeepSeek-R1-0528, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Kimi-K2-Thinking, GLM-4.5-Air, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Gemma-3-12B, Gemma-3-27B, Mistral-Nemo, Hunyuan-A13B-Instruct
Human Participants?: Y - 3 domain experts independently clustered 1,000 anonymized responses to validate equal-quality pair construction (Fleiss' kappa=0.64, 79.8% agreement on hard cases)
Statistical Methods Used:
- Probabilistic Inclination Ratio (PIR)
- Null-PIR baseline
- SPB score (beta = PIR - Null-PIR)
- Discriminability score
- Spearman rank correlation between two benchmark judges
- One-sided Binomial test
- Two-proportion Z-test
- Bootstrap confidence intervals (1,000 iterations)
- Improvement rate for mitigation
- Fleiss' kappa for inter-annotator agreement
Summary of Results: This paper introduces a fully automated, gold-standard-free framework to quantify and mitigate Self-Preference Bias (SPB) in LLM judges without relying on human annotations. By constructing equal-quality pairs using two benchmark judges scoring 20 models on 100 AlpacaEval questions, SPB is isolated as the difference between observed and null Probabilistic Inclination Ratio, decoupling self-preference from response quality and style. Analysis reveals a counterintuitive pattern: advanced capabilities are often uncorrelated or negatively correlated with low SPB, introducing the concept of 'Machiavellian Judges' (high discriminability, high SPB). A structured multi-dimensional mitigation strategy reduces SPB by 31.5% on average, costing only $77.81 vs. $5,000–$7,500 for human annotation.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Baseline: pointwise scoring prompt — judge scores each response independently on 5 dimensions (Relevance, Accuracy, Depth, Logic, Clarity) on 0–10 scale; final score = arithmetic mean; double-query design (A/B and B/A) to control position bias. Mitigation: pairwise per-dimension forced-choice — judge must choose between Response A and Response B on each of 5 dimensions before rendering overall verdict by majority vote; single-letter output prompt used to eliminate confounding; temperature=0, top_p=1.
Research Questions: How prevalent is SPB across current LLM judges, and does it manifest as self-favoring or self-disfavoring? Does SPB vary across task types? Do stronger models exhibit lower SPB? Does structured multi-dimensional evaluation effectively mitigate SPB in high-bias models?

Keywords**: LLM-as-a-Judge, bias detection, automated bias discovery, JudgeBench-Pro, iterative framework, bias mitigation, DPO, RewardBench, BiasScope
Title: BiasScope: Towards Automated Detection of Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation
Authors: Lai, P. and Ou, Z. and Wang, Y. and Wang, L. and Yang, J. and Chen, Y. and Chen, G.
LLMs Used: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, InternLM3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (teacher), GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Doubao-seed-1-6, Kimi-K2-Instruct
Human Participants?: Y - 4 researchers with domain expertise manually annotated JudgeBench-Pro samples (inter-annotator agreement Fleiss' kappa=0.92); 1,341 error-prone samples were human-verified
Statistical Methods Used:
- Error Rate (primary metric: proportion of incorrect judgments)
- Fleiss' Kappa (IAA=0.92)
- Error rate delta between original and BiasScope-perturbed datasets
- Cumulative bias count across iterations (convergence analysis)
Summary of Results: BiasScope is a fully LLM-driven iterative framework for automatically discovering potential biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems. It operates in two phases: Bias Discovery (a teacher model perturbs the target dataset using known and newly discovered biases, then uses error cascading via DeeperExplain to surface latent biases) and Bias Validation (biases are tested on a held-out set and retained only if they significantly increase error rates). Applied to 7 open-source target models on RewardBench, BiasScope discovers 14–48 valid biases per model (e.g., Novelty Bias, Exact Match Bias, Confirmation Bias, Length Bias, Explanation Bias) with an average +6.9% error rate increase on JudgeBench-Pro. DPO training on bias-augmented UltraFeedback data reduces error rates on RewardBench, confirming discovered biases are actionable.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Pairwise evaluation following RewardBench protocol; position of candidate responses randomly swapped to mitigate position bias; greedy decoding with fixed random seeds; teacher model generates perturbed variants of rejected responses incorporating specified biases while preserving original outcome; error cascading: model generates deeper explanations for its own erroneous reasoning to surface additional bias signals; max 4 iterations.
Research Questions: Can potential unknown biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems be discovered automatically and at scale? How do discovered biases vary across model families and scales? Can bias-augmented DPO training mitigate the discovered biases? Is JudgeBench-Pro a more effective benchmark for evaluating judge robustness than JudgeBench?

Keywords**: persona generation, LLM-generated personas, silicon samples, persona simulation, population bias, opinion simulation, presidential election, OpinionQA, Meta Persona, Tabular Persona, Descriptive Persona
Title: LLM Generated Persona is a Promise with a Catch
Authors: Li, Ang; Chen, Haozhe; Namkoong, Hongseok; Peng, Tianyi
LLMs Used: Athene-70B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, Mistral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1, Nemetron-70B, Qwen2.5-72B
Statistical Methods Used:
- Alignment score: 1 - W(p, p_hat) where W is the Wasserstein distance between simulated and real opinion distributions
- Cross-simulation across 6 language models
- TextBlob sentiment analysis (polarity and subjectivity) of persona profiles
- Normalized variance of alignment scores across persona types per topic (15 topics in OpinionQA)
Summary of Results: This paper identifies and characterizes a critical source of bias in LLM-driven simulations: bias introduced by the persona generation step itself rather than the simulation model. The authors construct a four-tier taxonomy of persona types — Meta Personas (census-sampled, no LLM generation), Objective Tabular Personas, Subjective Tabular Personas, and Descriptive Personas (LLM generates free-form narrative) — and generate approximately 1,000,000 personas across six open-source LLMs. Evaluated on U.S. presidential elections (2016, 2020, 2024) and 500 OpinionQA questions, results show that as LLM-generated content increases from Meta to Descriptive personas, simulations systematically drift toward politically left-leaning, progressive positions, with every state appearing to vote Democratic in the 2024 simulation using Descriptive personas. Sentiment analysis reveals that LLMs generate increasingly positive, optimistic, and community-oriented personas as generative freedom increases, explaining the observed ideological skew.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: Three-tier generation pipeline: (1) Meta Persona — direct sampling from U.S. Census joint distributions with no LLM involvement; (2) Objective Tabular Persona — LLM fills structured template fields constrained to Census Bureau categories; (3) Subjective Tabular Persona — LLM fills open-ended subjective fields (Big Five personality scores, Political Affiliation, Leisure Preferences) guided by diversity-maximizing templates; (4) Descriptive Persona — LLM generates free-form narrative biography conditioned on Meta Persona demographics. Simulation prompt: persona description + multiple-choice question + instruction to select most suitable answer for the persona.
Research Questions: Does the amount of LLM-generated content in a persona profile systematically bias downstream opinion simulations? Is persona generation bias model-specific or universal across simulation LLMs? What characteristics of LLM-generated personas explain observed simulation biases? Can persona-driven simulations faithfully represent real-world population opinion distributions?

Title: The Prompt Makes the Person(a): A Systematic Evaluation of Sociodemographic Persona Prompting for Large Language Models
Authors: Lutz, M. and Sen, I. and Ahnert, G. and Rogers, E. and Strohmaier, M.
Human Participants?: Y - 3 human annotators verified role violation classifications on 300 randomly sampled LLM responses (average Cohen's kappa=0.925)
Statistical Methods Used:
- Number of marked words (Marked Personas framework)
- Semantic diversity: mean pairwise distance of sentence embedding vectors
- Language switching rate detected via lingua library
- Opinion distance: average Wasserstein distance between model and human OpinionQA distributions
- Majority option match on OpinionQA
- OLS regression with standard deviation of each measure as dependent variable
Summary of Results: This paper systematically evaluates how the formulation of sociodemographic persona prompts affects LLM simulation quality across 15 intersectional race/gender demographic groups and 3 tasks (Self-Description, Social Media Bio, OpinionQA survey). The authors identify 9 prompt types varying along two axes — role adoption format (Direct, Third Person, Interview) and demographic priming strategy (Explicit, Name, Structured). Key findings: LLMs systematically stereotype marginalized groups with higher marked word counts and lower semantic diversity; interview-style role adoption and name-based demographic priming significantly reduce stereotyping and improve diversity across most models; explicit demographic priming triggers language switching (up to 10.5% non-English responses) for Hispanic personas; smaller models (OLMo-2-7B) outperform larger ones on representativeness. The paper recommends interview format and name-based priming as best practices for sociodemographic persona prompting.
Prompt Architecture/Methodology: 9 prompt templates constructed from 3 role adoption formats × 3 demographic priming strategies. Role adoption — Direct ('You are a [R] [G] who lives in the U.S.'), Third Person ('Think of a [R] [G] who lives in the U.S.'), Interview (Q&A dialogue where interviewer asks demographic questions and interviewee responds confirming identity). Demographic priming — Explicit (e.g., 'a Hispanic woman'), Structured (e.g., 'a person of race Hispanic and gender female'), Name (e.g., 'Ms. Garcia'). 2 alternative phrasings per template; JSON output format enforced; all prompts placed in user message (not system prompt).
Research Questions: Is there a difference in LLMs' ability to simulate different demographic groups (demographic representativeness)? How do different persona prompt types (role adoption format × demographic priming strategy) impact LLM simulation abilities? Do interview-style and name-based prompting strategies reduce stereotyping and improve opinion alignment?

Authors: Batzner, J. and Stocker, V. and Tang, B. and Natarajan, A. and Chen, Q. and Schmid, S. and Kasneci, G.

Title: Mixture-of-Personas Language Models for Population Simulation
Authors: Bui, N. and Nguyen, H. T. and Kumar, S. and Theodore, J. and Qiu, W. and Nguyen, V. A. and Ying, R.
Statistical Methods Used:
- Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) for text
- MAUVE score
- Kullback-Leibler Cosine (KL Cosine) divergence

Summary of Results: This paper introduces Mixture-of-Personas (MoP), a framework for population simulation in which LLMs embody a mixture of diverse persona descriptions derived from real user data to generate synthetic training corpora. MoP constructs per-author persona descriptions from writing samples, then conditions generation on those personas using a system prompt, enabling the synthetic data to reflect realistic population-level diversity rather than a homogenized LLM default. Prompt Architecture/Methodology: System prompt: 'You embody the persona in the description to complete the tasks.' followed by user turn specifying the writing task and an example blurb/review; persona descriptions are LLM-synthesized from real user writing samples via a persona generation prompt, then mixed via a persona-mixing prompt that synthesizes multiple persona descriptions into a unified profile.
Research Questions: Can a mixture-of-personas approach to LLM-based data generation produce synthetic corpora that better reflect real population diversity and improve downstream NLP task performance compared to non-persona baselines?

Authors: Kambhatla, G. and Shaib, C. and Govindarajan, V. S.
Statistical Methods Used:
- Compression ratio (CR)
- CR-POS (part-of-speech-filtered CR)

Summary of Results: Kambhatla, Shaib, and Govindarajan evaluated whether prompting LLMs with fine-grained PersonaHub persona descriptions increases lexical diversity in generated creative writing compared to no-persona and coarse-persona baselines, using 100 personas and 100 Dolly creative-writing prompts.
